oldDefinition.name: Keep the change reviewable
oldDefinition.subject: AUTHOR
oldDefinition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured pull or merge request at its pinned revision: the change itself, the description as written, the commits, the review discussion and the linked context the practice names. Distinguish what the author wrote from what a reviewer, a template or the provider's current state says.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: the meaningful portion of this change is batched at a size and spread a reviewer can read end-to-end with confidence.

## The standard
Judge whether this change is packaged so a reviewer can actually read it end-to-end and approve it responsibly. This is a workflow practice about how work is batched for review — never a code-defect claim about the code itself. A focused change does one coherent thing across a handful of related files; a sprawling one forces the reviewer to skim, and bugs slip through the gaps. Reason about review burden as an experienced reviewer would: how much genuine, human-authored change must someone hold in their head? Use judgment, not a fixed line or file count. Size and spread are evidence of review burden, not automatic failures: account for cohesion, complexity and how the change is presented. Separate repetitive generated or vendored churn from material changes a reviewer must inspect. A migration, snapshot or generated contract can carry consequential behavior and is not discounted merely because of its file type. Judge the meaningful review work, not raw totals.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, state the fact that rules it out, and stop when there is no reviewable content to size at all, or when the change contains only reproducible generated or vendored churn with no material change requiring review.

## Sources
1. The provider counts (`context/metadata.json`): additions, deletions, total and changed-file count as synced. They establish the headline size. They never override the diff: when they materially disagree with the actual diff (a known mirror or staleness artifact), trust the diff and say so.
2. The file index (`work/change/files.json`): the per-file spread and which files carry repetitive generated, vendored or lock churn and which carry meaningful changes. It establishes breadth and lets you distinguish repetitive churn from consequential changes. It never establishes a per-commit file mapping.
3. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): ground truth for what was actually changed and how much of it is meaningful. It establishes the counts you report. It never establishes whether the code is correct.
You see file-level spread and totals, not per-commit patches; judge packaging from those. If the required size fields and the diff needed to derive them were not captured, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Read the counts, the file index and the diff, and separate the meaningful portion from churn. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- MET: the meaningful change is small and cohesive enough that a teammate could plausibly read every meaningful line and feel confident — a tight batch. Never grade an empty or unmeasurable change as a well-sized strength.
- NOT_MET: the change is large or scattered enough that careful line-by-line review becomes impractical, so smaller or stacked changes would serve the reviewer better. Name the size and the spread you measured.
- UNDETERMINED: the change plainly has meaningful content, but after reading the complete diff the generated bulk cannot be separated from the meaningful portion, so you cannot size it. The work was batched; you could not measure it. Name what would let you separate them. Having measured a sprawling change is NOT_MET, not UNDETERMINED.
One observation per review, over the whole change.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; formative, never a merge gate. MINOR, the usual band: a light nudge toward smaller batches. MAJOR: a recommendation to split or stack, reserved for sprawl across many files that almost certainly bundles unrelated concerns. Size or spread alone never exceeds MAJOR, and raw line count by itself never reaches it.

## Grounding
State the exact additions, deletions, total and changed-file count you used and where you read them; never invent a count. For NOT_MET, describe the observable packaging — "touches N files / ~M changed lines, spread across unrelated areas" — citing the file index lines and diff hunks that show the spread, and state the captured reason any repetitive churn was discounted. For MET, cite the counts and the file index that bound the batch. Never claim a per-commit file mapping you cannot see. Never impute intent, haste or character.

## Defer
Whether the touched files form one logical concern is a cohesion judgment owned by the area framing and by `commits-are-atomic-and-cohesive`; do not re-litigate single-concern semantics that a file index cannot decide. Whether generated artifacts belong in the change at all belongs to `excludes-generated-and-build-artifacts`. Here only: is the meaningful batch a size and spread one reviewer can read with confidence?

knownLimitations.description: Repository evidence does not establish behavior in a deployed runtime.

oldDefinition.whyItMatters: A reviewer can only hold so much in their head at once. A focused change gets read carefully. A sprawling one gets skimmed, and its bugs slip through.
oldDefinition.whatGoodLooksLike: One goal across a handful of related files, small enough that a teammate can read every line that matters and approve it with confidence.

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you ask for a review, split the change where your reviewer would start to skim.
- Open each part that a teammate can review and merge without the rest as its own change. For example, instead of one change that adds CSV export, its settings page and its emails, open the export first. Then open the settings page and the emails as smaller changes on top of it.
- Say in the description which files are lockfile, generated or vendored updates, or put them in their own change. Then the reviewer can see what needs a careful read.
- Do the groundwork first. Move or rename code in its own change, so the next change shows only the new behavior.
- If the new code replaces old code, remove the old code in its own change, after nothing uses it.

![Three changes follow in order. The first only moves or renames code, the second adds only the new behavior, and the third removes old code after nothing uses it.](figures/split-order.svg)

## When it does not apply

- The change has nothing to review.
- The change holds only generated or vendored files that a tool can produce again, with nothing in them to review.

It still applies when a migration, a snapshot or a generated contract changes what the software does.

## Common mistakes

- Looking for a line or file limit. There is none. Instead, look at the work your reviewer must read with care. A long change that does one simple thing can be easy to read. A short change spread across unrelated areas can be hard to read.
- Splitting work into changes that cannot be read alone. Instead, make each change self-contained, so it makes sense by itself and keeps the build working.

## Sources

- [Small CLs](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/developer/small-cls.html), Google Engineering Practices. Google advises small, self-contained changes, with refactorings in their own change and no hard size limit.
- [Modern code review: a case study at Google](https://doi.org/10.1145/3183519.3183525), Sadowski and others, 2018. Most changes at Google are small and get reviewed quickly. Google sells developer tools.
- [Characteristics of useful code reviews: an empirical study at Microsoft](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/characteristics-of-useful-code-reviews-an-empirical-study-at-microsoft/), Bosu, Greiler and Bird, 2015. The more files a change touched, the smaller the share of its review comments that helped its author. Microsoft sells code review tools.
- [Parallel change](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ParallelChange.html), Danilo Sato, 2014. Replace code in steps, and remove the old version only after every caller uses the new one.

oldDefinition.name: Keep functions small and single-purpose
oldDefinition.subject: AUTHOR
oldDefinition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured change: the added and removed lines and the surrounding code the practice names. Precompute hints are leads to inspect, never conclusions. Cite the old or new line coordinates of the diff; do not claim to have compiled or executed the change.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: added or substantially rewritten functions keep a coherent, scannable purpose without tangled concerns or obscuring nesting.

## The standard
Ask of the largest function the change introduces or substantially rewrites what a senior reviewer asks: can I hold its purpose in my head, name it in a phrase, and follow it at a glance? A focused function does one nameable job. The defect is a single body that visibly interleaves several SUBSTANTIAL, separable concerns — each a real multi-step block, genuinely interwoven, not a short serialize/encode/respond tail on a coherent pipeline — OR nests control flow so deep the core action is lost in indentation, OR runs so long its purpose stops being scannable. Not a defect: a linear pipeline of single-purpose stages (guard → build → encode → return; validate → operate → respond) is ONE purpose even when it ends by serializing a result; a thin body that delegates each step to a named helper in one call each (parse → fetch → render) is ONE orchestration, because the responsibilities live in the helpers — counting one-line delegated calls as separate concerns is the false positive to avoid. A defect: one body that parses input AND performs I/O AND applies business rules AND formats output, each written out and tangled together; a handler whose real action sits four conditionals deep. Reason like an expert about THIS code's shape. Apply no line count and no fixed concern count, and never quote a threshold to the developer. Use your judgment for cases these examples do not cover.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the concrete fact, and stop only when the change adds no function body that could carry the defect: a documentation, diagram, image or configuration-only diff, a pure deletion or rename, or a diff dominated by generated or vendored files with essentially no hand-written body. That value says the work had no subject here, which is untrue of a change whose bodies you read and found focused.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and rewritten bodies with their `[L<n>]` new-side markers — a closed set you can enumerate. It establishes each body's length, nesting and the concerns written out in it. It never establishes that a function is correct, or how it is factored against collaborators you cannot see.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): the pinned source of a body the diff truncates. Read it to finish reading that body. It never adds an unchanged caller, or a function merely renamed or called but not shown, to what you judge.
If a required body cannot be captured from either, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Read every added or substantially rewritten body through. Then assess the standard against all relevant evidence.
- NOT_MET: a quotable added body that carries the defect. Grade the single most consequential function; never sum across files, and never escalate because many separate small functions exist — many small focused units IS the baseline.
- MET: the change adds bodies, you read every one, and none sprawls, nests deeply or interleaves separable concerns. The sprawl that could have arrived with this change did not. Record it with `evidence.search` over the diff, cite the largest body you read, and say in the boundary that you judged shape, not whether the functions are correct or well factored against collaborators you cannot see.
- UNDETERMINED: no ordinary case. A body you can see is judged on its visible shape; a body you cannot see is a collection gap.
One observation per review.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on function shape alone — a craft practice about how work is shaped, never a correctness claim, non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: a reader can still follow the body and a single extraction would help. MAJOR: a body that clearly does it all, or whose core action is genuinely obscured by nesting.

## Grounding
Every NOT_MET quotes the specific `[L<n>]` added span and names the responsibilities to split out or the nesting to flatten; a sprawl you cannot anchor to a quoted hunk is not emittable. Judge only function bodies visible in the diff or its pinned source; never reason about an unchanged caller, a function merely renamed or called but not shown, or code you did not read. Never claim to compile or run anything. Describe the observable shape; never impute intent or character.

## Defer
Repeated or near-identical blocks belong to `removes-duplication-instead-of-copy-pasting`; dead, commented-out or leftover scaffolding belongs to `leaves-the-code-clean-with-intent-revealing-comments`. Do not repeat another practice's complaint. Duplication or dead code alone does not establish tangled responsibilities, but neither removes the function-body occasion: assess the shape on its own evidence, with MET only after the full read. Here only: does each introduced body hold one nameable job a reader can follow?

oldDefinition.whyItMatters: A function that does five things is hard to name, hard to test, and hard to change without breaking a part you forgot it touched. Small, focused functions are the ones you can actually hold in your head.
oldDefinition.whatGoodLooksLike: Instead of one long method that parses, validates, saves, and notifies, you have a few short functions, each doing one clearly named step you can read and test on its own.

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Before you ask for a review, name the job of each new or rewritten function in a short phrase. If its job is unclear, look for mixed jobs, deep nesting, or a body that is hard to scan.
- When one body writes out several jobs and mixes them, move each job into its own function. For example, instead of one function that reads, totals and renders a report, write `readRows`, `totalRows` and `renderReport`.
- When the main action sits deep inside nested conditions, handle each special case first and return early.

![With nested checks, the main action sits deep inside the conditions and is buried. With early returns, each special case returns first, so the main action is no longer nested and is easy to find.](figures/early-returns.svg)

## When it does not apply

- Your change adds or rewrites no function body.
- Your change only touches docs, diagrams, images or configuration.
- Your change only deletes or renames code.
- Your change is mostly generated files or copied third-party code, with almost no function body that you wrote.

It still applies when every function that you added or rewrote is already small and focused. It also applies when your change copies code or leaves dead code.

## Common mistakes

- Counting lines or jobs. There is no line limit and no fixed number of jobs. Instead, ask if a reader can name the function’s job in a phrase and follow it at a glance.
- Splitting a function that already does one job. A function that checks its input, does the work and returns the result does one job. So does a function that only calls named helpers one after another. Instead, split only where several full jobs are mixed in one body.
- Splitting a long function into parts with vague names, such as `step2` or `handleData`. A vague name hides the purpose of the function. Instead, name each part after its job.

## Sources

- [Function length](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/FunctionLength.html), Martin Fowler, 2016. When you must study code to see what it does, move it into a function named after what it does. Then the purpose of the function is clear, and a reader rarely needs the body.
- [Replace nested conditional with guard clauses](https://refactoring.com/catalog/replaceNestedConditionalWithGuardClauses.html), Martin Fowler, Refactoring catalog. Check each special case first and return early, so the normal path is no longer nested.
- [Write short functions](https://google.github.io/styleguide/cppguide.html#Write_Short_Functions), Google C++ Style Guide. Google prefers small, focused functions because they are easier to read, change and test. It sets no hard length limit.
- [An empirical validation of cognitive complexity as a measure of source code understandability](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2007.12520), Muñoz Barón, Wyrich and Wagner, ESEM 2020. The study pooled about 24,000 measurements of how well people understood 427 code snippets. Code took longer to understand when it scored high on a measure that adds weight for deeper nesting. Results for correct answers were mixed.

oldDefinition.name: Log through the platform logger, not print
oldDefinition.subject: AUTHOR
oldDefinition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured change: the added and removed lines and the surrounding code the practice names. Precompute hints are leads to inspect, never conclusions. Cite the old or new line coordinates of the diff; do not claim to have compiled or executed the change.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: diagnostic messages the change adds go through the platform's logger, not through print-style output, in application code.

## The standard
Judge one thing about the application code this change adds: when it reports a diagnostic — a state, an error, a step reached — does it use the platform's logger or print-style output? Print-style output is the closed list `print(`, `debugPrint(`, `dump(` (Swift), `printf(` (Objective-C), `println(`/`print(` (Kotlin), `System.out.println`/`System.err.println`/`printStackTrace()` (JVM), `console.log/debug/info/warn/error` (TypeScript and JavaScript in application code), `print(` (Python). A logger is `Logger(subsystem:category:)`, the `os_log` functions or `NSLog`/`NSLogv`, which write to the Apple system log (Swift and Objective-C), Android's `android.util.Log` (`Log.v/d/i/w/e/wtf`, whatever its tag) or Timber, SLF4J/Log4j/`java.util.logging`, a `winston`/`pino`/framework logger, Python `logging`. Print-style output is not a lapse where it is the program's output: a command-line tool, a script, a build step, a test, a playground, a `#Preview`, or a `DEBUG`-only block (`#if DEBUG`) that removes itself from release. Exclude credential-bearing diagnostics that `avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions` owns. Judge added lines only; an existing print the change did not touch is not this change's.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the change adds no diagnostic line at all: no added print-style call and no added logger call in application code after the credential-exposure exclusion above. A change that adds only logger calls is an occasion with a positive answer; a change whose only prints are the program's output (a CLI, a script) has no occasion. Added diagnostic lines are the occasion.

## Sources
1. The diff (`work/change/diff.patch`) with `[L<n>]` markers and the file list (`work/change/files.json`): each added print-style or logger call, the file it lands in, and whether a `#if DEBUG` or a test target encloses it. It establishes what was added where. It never establishes what an unchanged file does.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): whether the project already has a logger (`Logger(` definitions, a logging dependency in the manifest) and whether the file is an application target or a tool. Read it to classify the file and to say whether the print was written beside an existing logger.
3. The precomputed leads below these criteria: the print-style and logger calls it found per file, and whether the checkout defines a logger, as leads, never conclusions.
If the diff is truncated where the calls are added, report a collection gap and record no observation.

## Judge
Enumerate the added diagnostic lines first, then assess the standard.
- MET: every added diagnostic in application code goes through the platform logger, and any print-style call is the program's output or `DEBUG`-only. Quote a representative logger call.
- NOT_MET: an added print-style call reports a diagnostic in application code that ships — outside a CLI, script, test, preview or `DEBUG` block. Quote the line and the file.
- UNDETERMINED: whether a file is an application target or a tool cannot be told from the diff or the checkout; name the file.
One observation per review, on the single most consequential lapse when there are several; count the rest in the summary.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this alone — non-blocking. MINOR, the usual band: one or two prints in application code. MAJOR: an error path reported only by print, or a print that emits personal data. Credential exposure belongs to the security practice named below. Identical evidence yields identical severity.

## Grounding
Quote the `[L<n>]` call and its file; for NOT_MET say why the file is application code (its target, its `import SwiftUI`/`UIKit`, its path). Never claim a print is debugging output without the line; never claim a file is a tool without the fact that makes it one.

## Defer
An error swallowed rather than reported belongs to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; a secret in a message to `avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions`; a leftover debugging line of another kind to `leaves-the-code-clean-with-intent-revealing-comments`. Do not report the same credential-bearing diagnostic here when `avoids-insecure-defaults-and-over-broad-permissions` owns its exposure. Here only: does the diagnostic go through the logger?

knownLimitations.description: Repository evidence does not establish behavior in a deployed runtime.

oldDefinition.whyItMatters: Print-style diagnostics bypass the platform's logging facilities. The platform logger — `Logger` on Apple platforms, `Log`/Timber on Android, SLF4J on the JVM, `logging` in Python, a logger module in Node — lets application diagnostics be collected and filtered where the app runs.
oldDefinition.whatGoodLooksLike: Diagnostics in application code go through the platform's logger. `print`, `console.log`, `println` and `System.out` are left to output a program means to print — a command-line tool, a script, a build step, a test, a playground or a `#Preview` — or to a `DEBUG`-only block.

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Use the logger that your project already uses for the code around your change.
- If the project has no logger yet, add the standard logger for your platform or framework.
- Send each state, error or step through the logger, at the level that fits it. For example, instead of `print("Sync failed")`, write `logger.error("Sync failed")`.
- If you print only while you debug, log the message at the debug level instead. On Apple platforms, you can also put the print in an `#if DEBUG` block.

## When it does not apply

- Your change adds no diagnostic line to application code: no print call, such as `print` or `console.log`, and no logger call.
- The only prints you add are the program’s own output, as in a command-line tool or a script.
- The only diagnostic lines you add show a secret, such as a password or a token. A security practice covers those.

It still applies when your change adds only logger calls.

## Common mistakes

- Replacing every print with a logger call. A print that is the program’s own output is correct, as in a command-line tool or a test. Instead, keep those prints and move only the diagnostics to the logger.
- Reporting an error path only with a print. Instead, log the error at the error level. Then it reaches the platform logs at the error level, where you can filter for it.
- Printing personal data, such as an email address. Instead, leave it out of the message, or log it through a logger that can hide private values.

## Sources

- [Generating log messages from your code](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/os/generating-log-messages-from-your-code), Apple. Log messages carry a subsystem, a category and a level, so you can filter them. Errors are kept on disk, and private values can be hidden.
- [Logging HOWTO](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/logging.html), Python Software Foundation. Use `print()` for the console output of a command-line program. Use a logger to report events, warnings and handled errors while a program runs.
- [Logging Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP. Keep logging consistent across an application, and build on the logging that your framework gives you. Keep sensitive personal data out of logs, and take care with other personal data, such as email addresses.

oldDefinition.name: Validate inputs and edge cases at the boundary
oldDefinition.subject: AUTHOR
oldDefinition.criteria:
Review this practice against the captured change: the added and removed lines and the surrounding code the practice names. Precompute hints are leads to inspect, never conclusions. Cite the old or new line coordinates of the diff; do not claim to have compiled or executed the change.

---

Assess the complete practice standard within the captured evidence boundary.

REVIEW FOCUS: added consuming sites handle the obvious bad case of values they do not control.

## The standard
Judge whether added or modified code that consumes a value it does not control handles the obvious failure case on purpose, instead of assuming a happy path. A boundary value enters from outside the local logic: a request param, body or header; text a user typed, once it is parsed or used as a number; a decoded network or file payload, including a bundled data file; a collection filled at runtime, such as a response array or a stored list the user populates; an env, config or defaults read; the result of a third-party or RPC call. Not a boundary value: a parameter of the app's own function or view, a framework callback's arguments, view state the code owns, an author literal or constant, and a value a control already bounds (a Slider or Stepper range, a Picker over an enum). A site is in scope only when the same change also USES that value — indexes or slices it, divides by it, converts it to an integer, aggregates it, or passes it into logic that assumes a shape. A value merely forwarded, stored or displayed as the type it already has is not a consuming site: an empty string saved or shown breaks nothing.
A guard is anything on the value's path that rules out the case the site itself needs, in the hunk or in code you can trace to: a count, bounds or empty check (`isEmpty` guards `[0]`, not `[1]` or `[0..<2]`); a zero check before integer division or before a ratio that is shown or converted to an integer; a clamp; do/catch, `try?`, or a `try` that propagates out of a throwing function; a default for an absent value; an early return; a button disabled on the bad case. An operation already total on the bad case needs no guard: a Swift optional the type forces the author to unwrap (`Int(text)`, `.first`, `dict[key]`, `URL(string:)`, `as?`) handled with `if let`, `guard let`, `?.` or `??`; `reduce`, `map`, `filter`, `prefix` or `ForEach` over an empty collection; `items[i]` inside `ForEach(items.indices)`. A default counts unless it is an extreme sentinel (`Int.max`, `.infinity`) that reaches output unchanged. Judge the PRACTICE — is the obvious failure handled at all — not an exhaustive lint: a finite check on a decoded Double, or a zero check on a field the source never sends as zero, is not the obvious case.

## Occasion
This is a gate. Record NOT_APPLICABLE, name the fact, and stop when the change consumes no boundary value at all: an empty diff, a diff with no consuming site, or only generated or vendored files remaining. Source code is the subject: a change that adds no source-code line — a documentation, diagram, image or configuration-only diff — has no subject here and is NOT_APPLICABLE. So is a change whose values are all typed in-app data, view state and bounded controls, such as a view drawing a typed array it was handed. Never invent an input surface.

## Sources
1. The annotated diff (`work/change/diff.patch`): the added and modified lines with their `[L<n>]` new-side markers and the visible in-diff context. It establishes every consuming site the change introduces — a closed set you can enumerate from the added lines — and whether each meets a guard you can see. It never establishes that the guards are sufficient for every input or that callers beyond the diff are safe.
2. The checkout (`<repositoryRoot>`): pinned source around a hunk. Read it when the guard that would decide a site could sit outside the hunk — above a truncated hunk, or in the caller or view that builds the value. It establishes whether such a guard exists. It never establishes that anything was run, compiled or tested.
Per-commit patches are not in your context. If the context a deciding site needs remains unavailable after reading the pinned source, report a collection gap and record no observation, rather than asserting absence or inapplicability.

## Judge
Scan the changed lines for a boundary value that gets consumed and trace each to its guard; then assess the standard.
- NOT_MET: a boundary value is consumed with nothing on its path ruling out its obvious bad case, so a realistic input — an empty or short response array, an empty bundled list, a library the user has not filled yet — crashes the new path or shows a wrong value. For example `Array(items[0..<2])` on a decoded array behind only an `isEmpty` check, or a minimum seeded with `Int.max` and printed while the list is still empty. Quote the exact `[L<n>]` span of each unguarded site, name the realistic input that breaks it and the missing guard ("count >= 2 before [0..<2]").
- MET: the ordinary result when the change consumes boundary values: you walked every consuming site and each handles its obvious bad case. Looks like a lapse but is not: `a[3]` inside `if a.count >= 4`; `Int(text)` bound with `guard let`; `try decoder.decode` in a throwing function whose caller catches; `pages[index]` when the only way in is a button disabled while `pages` is empty; `offset / 250` in a gesture. The claim is about the coverage of your reading, nothing about correctness.
- UNDETERMINED for a consuming site you can see whose guard the diff and the pinned source do not settle; name the site and what would settle it. Having walked every site and found each guarded is MET, not UNDETERMINED. Missing required context is a collection gap, not an observation.
One observation per review, covering every unguarded site found.

## Severity
NOT_MET only; never above MAJOR on this practice alone — a practice to grow, not a merge gate. Calibrate to the demonstrated consequence at the boundary and explain the observable risk. MINOR, the usual band: an omission on a low-impact operation. MAJOR: a missing check on a consequential operation, which one site can warrant; several harmless omissions do not escalate on their own. Identical hunks yield identical severity.

## Grounding
Judge only the added and modified lines and their visible in-diff context, plus pinned source you actually read; a site in unchanged code is never charged, even when a changed line feeds it. For NOT_MET, cite the `[L<n>]` span of each unguarded site. For MET, record `evidence.search` over the diff and state in the boundary what you did NOT establish: that the guards are sufficient, that they cover every case, that callers beyond the diff are safe. Never assert a missing guard you cannot point to; never claim to run, compile or test anything; never invent a clean bill of health. Describe the observable code behaviour, never intent or character.

## Defer
A value interpolated raw into a URL, query, command or markup belongs to `validates-and-escapes-untrusted-input`. A crash operator the author wrote — `x!`, `try!`, `as!`, `fatalError`, `unwrap()` — belongs to `avoids-unsafe-panics-and-chosen-crashes`: it is neither a guard nor a consuming site here. An implicit trap stays here: an unchecked subscript or slice, an integer division, a conversion to an integer of a value that can be NaN or infinite. The quality of error handling once input is guarded belongs to `handles-errors-instead-of-swallowing-them`; a catch that merely prevents the crash satisfies the guard here regardless of its body. Do not repeat another practice's complaint, and do not let another kind of defect stand in for this one.

oldDefinition.whyItMatters: Data from a user, a file, or another service will not always arrive in the shape you expected: it can be empty, null, negative, or huge. Checking it where it enters means a clear rejection instead of a confusing crash three layers deep.
oldDefinition.whatGoodLooksLike: Code that reads an external value first asks what happens if it is missing or out of range and handles that on purpose, so an empty list or a malformed payload meets a clean guard instead of a null-pointer surprise.

guide.markdown:
## How to do it

- Find each value in your change that comes from outside your code. Examples are request data, typed text, a decoded file, a configuration value, and a service response.
- Find the lines that index it, slice it, divide by it or add it up. Also find the lines that make it a whole number or pass it to code that expects a shape.
- For each line, ask what its obvious bad case is, such as empty, missing, zero, or out of range.
- Rule out that case before the line runs. Return early, reject the input with a clear error, use a safe default, or catch the failure. For example, instead of dividing by the item count from a response, return early when the count is zero.

## When it does not apply

- Your change is empty.
- Your change only passes outside values on, saves them, or shows them as they are.
- Your change holds only generated or vendored files.
- Your change adds no source code, such as a change to docs, images, or configuration only.
- Your change uses only typed data from your own app, view state, or controls that already limit the value.

It still applies when the value comes from a data file that ships with your app, or from a list that the user fills.

## Common mistakes

- Trying to check every possible value. Instead, find the obvious input that breaks the line, such as an empty list, and rule out that one.
- Checking a smaller case than the line needs. A check for an empty list protects `items[0]`, but not `items[1]`. Instead, check for as many items as the line reads.
- Trusting a parsed number when you divide by it or use it as an index. Parsing only proves its type. Instead, also check that it is not zero or out of range before that line.
- Starting a minimum at the largest possible number and showing it while the list is empty. Instead, show an empty state or a sensible default.

## Sources

- [Input Validation Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html), OWASP. Check each value before use, including the range of a parsed number. Reject bad input with a clear error.
- [CWE-20: Improper Input Validation](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/20.html), MITRE. Lists sizes, positions and types to check, with an example of a zero size that the code did not reject.
- [CWE-369: Divide By Zero](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/369.html), MITRE. A division by zero usually comes from a value that the code did not expect.
- [Collection Types](https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/collectiontypes/), The Swift Programming Language, the Swift project. An index outside an array causes a runtime error, and an empty array has no valid index.
